content: R. Squibb Corporation, based in New York City, had Peter R. Dolan as its Chairman and CEO until September 2006. Dolan was dismissed due to his handling of a patent dispute involving the drug Plavix. He was replaced by James Cornelius, who initially served as interim CEO but later assumed the permanent roles of CEO and Chairman following the retirement of James Robinson III. Robinson had been appointed Chairman as part of a settlement related to the channel-stuffing scandal. The company faced significant challenges during the 2000s due to a series of scandals, including channel-stuffing, which led to over $1 billion in state and federal fines. To avoid federal prosecution, Bristol-Myers Squibb (BMS) was placed under the oversight of a federal judge, and former FBI director Louis Freeh was appointed to the Board of Directors for a two-year period. Additionally, Richard Lane, the former head of the Pharma group, and Fred Schiff, the ex-CFO, were indicted for federal securities violations. BMS's primary research and development (R&D) facilities are located in Lawrenceville, New Jersey (formerly Squibb), and Wallingford, Connecticut (formerly Bristol-Myers), with additional sites across the U.S., Ireland, and other countries. Under Cornelius's leadership, the company embarked on a mission to sell itself while implementing a major restructuring plan. This plan focused on biologic products and included cost-cutting measures such as a 20% reduction in headcount over three years, primarily through layoffs, outsourcing, and offshoring operations. A significant shift was made to replace U.S.-based R&D with more cost-effective operations in India and China. In 2005, BMS was one of 53 entities that contributed the maximum allowable $250,000 to President George W. Bush's second inauguration. The company is a Fortune 500 entity, ranked 129 on the 2007 list. Bristol-Myers Squibb manufactures prescription pharmaceuticals and healthcare products across various therapeutic areas. It is also the parent company of Mead Johnson, which produces nutritional products like Enfamil baby formulas and infant vitamin supplements such as Tri-Vi-Sol, as well as ConvaTec, a global leader in ostomy and wound care products. The company’s mission is to Extend and Enhance Human Life by addressing unmet medical needs. Lance Armstrong, a testicular cancer survivor treated with BMS medication, has appeared in several of the company’s marketing campaigns. Key Pharmaceutical Products: Abilify (aripiprazole) ATRIPLA (efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) Avalide (irbesartan/hydrochlorothiazide) Avapro (irbesartan) Baraclude (entecavir) Cardiolite (technetium Tc99m sestamibi injection kit) Erbitux (cetuximab) Ixempra (ixabepilone) Orencia (abatacept) Plavix (clopidogrel bisulfate) Pravachol (pravastatin sodium) Reyataz (atazanavir sulfate) Sprycel (dasatinib) Sustiva (efavirenz) Taxol (paclitaxel) Videx EC (didanosine, delayed-release capsules) Zerit (stavudine) Taxol: At one point, BMS held the exclusive contract to harvest the bark of endangered yew trees in the U.S. for the production of the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel (Taxol). Current production of paclitaxel now relies on renewable sources. While BMS originally held the paclitaxel license, there are now multiple generic producers. Products Under Development: Ipilimumab Belatacept Saxagliptin Apixaban Pexacerfont Dapagliflozin Scandals and Allegations: On June 30, 1999, consumer advocate Ralph Nader testified before the House Budget Committee on corporate welfare, highlighting that Taxol was largely developed by the federal government while BMS retained production rights, potentially earning over $1 billion annually. In 2002, BMS was involved in an accounting scandal that required a significant restatement of revenues from 1999 to 2001. This was due to improper booking of sales related to channel-stuffing, a practice of offering excess inventory to customers to inflate sales figures. The company later settled with the U.S. Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission, agreeing to pay $150 million without admitting or denying guilt. In 2003, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) filed a consent order against the company, and state attorneys general sued to recover monetary damages. A criminal investigation into the company became public in July 2006, leading to an FBI raid on its corporate offices. The investigation focused on the distribution of Plavix and allegations of collusion. On September 12, 2006, a federal monitor, former Judge Frederick B. Lacey, recommended the removal of then-CEO Peter Dolan over the Plavix dispute. Under Cornelius’s leadership, all executives involved in the channel-stuffing and generic competition scandals have since left the company. The most recent departure was Andrew Bodner, Executive Vice President, who was indicted for his role in the Plavix-Apotex episode.
